subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: rationalising the wrongdoing as common practice [Pitfall]
passage:
Month-end, Friday. In the sales office, Lokesh leaned over the desk. "Everyone rounds the figures up a bit, Seema. Nobody's hurt. It's how the game works." Seema had hesitated, then added a small amount to her own total. Nothing happened.
Three months later. The small amounts had grown, always "just to match last month". Seema's stomach twisted each time she pressed save, but the twist was getting weaker.
Quarter-end, Wednesday. The auditors asked why the figures did not match the bank records. Seema's name was on every changed sheet. Lokesh stared at his screen and said nothing. Seema was called into the manager's room, and the door closed behind her.

qa.q: Whose name was on every changed sheet?
qa.a: Seema's name was on every changed sheet.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling each time she pressed save in the second beat?
qa.a: Seema felt a twisting unease that was already growing weaker, as the habit made it seem normal.

qa.q: What could Seema have done in the first month when the rounding began?
qa.a: Seema could have refused to change the figures and asked the manager how totals should be recorded.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt when the auditors asked their questions?
qa.a: Lokesh was probably scared and wanted to avoid blame, as staring at the screen in silence suggests.

grounding: The passage shows an employee who copies colleagues' claim that everyone shaves numbers, so that small compromises grow until an audit shows a serious problem.

subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: rationalising the wrongdoing as common practice [Pitfall]
passage: Tarun, you said today, 'Everyone rounds the sales numbers up a bit.' I said the same thing once. Sit, let your Sabina ma'am tell you how that ended. I was twenty-five, new in a medicine sales team. My senior showed me how to add a few 'visits' to doctors we hadn't met. 'Everyone does it,' he said. So I did it too. Three visits a month. It felt like nothing. The next year, ten. Then we were adding samples we hadn't given, and orders that didn't exist. By my third year, the team's numbers were built on air. An audit came. Four of us lost our jobs, and I spent two years explaining my record in every interview. Nobody remembered that 'everyone' did it. They remembered my name on the reports.

qa.q: How many visits a month did Sabina add at first?
How did Sabina feel about the first small additions?
qa.a: At first she felt comfortable, even unbothered, because 'everyone does it' made the additions seem like nothing.

qa.q: Where in Sabina's story was the best moment to stop?
qa.a: The very first time her senior showed her, because refusing three fake visits was far easier than undoing a record built on air.

qa.q: How might the senior who taught Sabina have been affected by the audit?
qa.a: He likely faced the same audit and job loss, since the habit he passed on became part of the team's whole record.

grounding: It shows a young employee copying colleagues who say everyone adjusts numbers, with small compromises growing until an audit exposes a serious problem.

passage:
In the quarter's last week, the delivery targets were impossible, and the Kochi office hummed with tired people. Francis leaned over Harsha's screen. 'Just mark it on time. It's one day late. Everyone does it; the client never checks.' Harsha hesitated, then clicked 'on time'. It was only one shipment.
Next quarter, it was twelve. Harsha told herself what Francis had said: everyone does it. By the third quarter, the team was marking whole weeks of delays as on time, and the client's warehouse, planning around those dates, ran out of stock during a festival sale.
The client's audit took two days. On the third, Harsha sat in a meeting room with HR, looking at a spreadsheet with her own login beside two hundred entries.

qa.q: How many shipments were marked on time in the next quarter?
What was Harsha feeling in the meeting room with HR?
qa.a: She was likely frightened and ashamed, seeing her own login beside two hundred false entries.

qa.q: What other approach could Harsha have taken with the first late shipment?
qa.a: She could have marked it late and told her manager the targets were unrealistic, so the problem was visible instead of hidden.

qa.q: How was the client affected by the habit?
qa.a: The client planned around false dates and ran out of stock during a festival sale, losing sales and trust.

grounding: It shows an employee copying the 'everyone does it' reasoning about late deliveries, with small compromises growing into a serious problem that an audit exposes.
